ActiveEvidence: Decision-Focused Evidence Graphs with Verifiable Acquisition Gaps

CCS: Computing methodologies Artificial intelligenceCCS: Computing methodologies Planning and schedulingCCS: Information systems Multimedia information systems
Miaobo Hu1,2, Shuhao Hu2, Xiaobo Guo2, Xin Wang2
Bokun Wang2, Peng Zhang2, Daren Zha2, Jun Xiao1,∗
1School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
2Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
∗Corresponding author: xiaojun@ucas.ac.cn
© none
Abstract.

A multimodal agent must decide whether visual evidence is worth acquiring, which candidate or resolution to query, and when further interaction can no longer change its decision. We study this problem under a strict free-metadata/paid-observation boundary, stochastic vector costs, and a frozen execution trace, and treat it as decision-certifiable active evidence acquisition. A Counterfactual Evidence Interaction Graph (CEIG) represents unary evidence value, signed second-order interaction, and directed conditional harm while maintaining explicit score enclosures for unresolved interactions; a decision-weighted enclosure objective tightens the bounds that can change action identity. Gap-directed refinement evaluates only interactions that can displace the incumbent acquisition and stops once an ϵ\epsilon-decision certificate shows that unresolved terms cannot change the selected action beyond a declared tolerance. The certificate is model-relative: it verifies policy-consistent optimality under the pinned learned score, and semantic quality is measured separately through post-freeze labels. Paired continuation rollouts learn the downstream value of paid previews, an online operational cost filter is separated from independent finite-policy-family trajectory certification, and an acquisition monitor with an independently implemented verifier binds every certificate to the frozen trace. On 640 cases split into 384/128/128 training, validation, and test cases, the controller reaches task score 0.842, grounding F1 0.816, evidence recall 0.873, 1.74 accepted calls, 286.5K visual tokens, and 742ms p95 latency. Dense replay of issued certificates shows 0.992 action agreement and a 0.988 certificate rate while evaluating 19.6 instead of 191.4 expensive interaction terms per decision.

Keywords: 
Multimodal agents, Active evidence acquisition, Resource-bounded decision making, Replayable evaluation

1. Introduction

A multimodal agent receives a user request, a candidate pool of visual evidence served through a metered acquisition interface, and an explicit resource budget. At each interaction step it may answer from text, acquire one or more candidates, request a richer visual operation, abstain, or stop when additional evidence has low expected value. Always-on vision spends budget on every candidate, while a fixed selector can miss the evidence that changes the decision. We study this as sequential evidence acquisition with an information boundary: the online policy sees selection-time fields and the acquired observations, while task labels and post-hoc usefulness labels enter only after the trace is frozen.

Prior tool-using agents make the action–observation loop explicit (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023), and grounded web agents show why realistic interfaces and functional evaluation matter (Deng et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024). The remaining gap is a measurable whether–which–when decision over multiple visual candidates and resource budgets, with an execution trace that preserves the information boundary.

Adaptive acquisition leaves three agent-level questions open. Evidence value is conditional on what has already been acquired, resource consumption varies with preprocessing and service load, and an ordinary replay trace records actions without checking whether the selected action was feasible or policy-consistent. Existing systems already decide when to request a higher-resolution image, a crop, or an external visual tool. ActiveEvidence targets a different question: when has an agent computed enough of the evidence-interaction structure to justify a particular acquisition decision? Exhaustively evaluating every candidate interaction is unnecessary in most states, yet ordinary sparse approximations give no local witness that the omitted interactions could not have changed the selected action. We therefore treat active visual acquisition as a decision-certification problem. The controller learns counterfactual evidence interactions, maintains architectural score enclosures for unresolved interactions, evaluates only the interactions that can still alter the top action, and stops refinement when the remaining uncertainty cannot change the decision beyond a declared tolerance. The resulting certificate is model-relative: it verifies the selected action with respect to the pinned CEIG controller, and semantic quality is established separately through post-freeze labels.

Contributions.

  • •

    We formulate decision-certifiable active evidence acquisition as a sequential agent decision under a strict boundary between free metadata and paid observations, vector-valued budgets, separate STOP/ABSTAIN terminal states, and an externally committed trace-freeze boundary.

  • •

    We introduce a decision-certifiable CEIG that separates unary utility, signed second-order interaction, directed conditional harm, and semantic contradiction, and train it with a decision-weighted enclosure objective so that interaction bounds are tightest on the edges that can change the acquisition decision.

  • •

    We introduce gap-directed interaction refinement: the controller refines only interactions that can displace the incumbent action, prioritizes them by their potential incumbent–challenger gap reduction, and terminates with an ϵ\epsilon-decision certificate relative to the pinned dense controller (Proposition 3.2).

  • •

    We learn paid-preview value from paired continuation decisions and separate online operational cost filtering from finite-policy-family trajectory certification (Proposition 3.4); monitor receipts and cross-implementation replay distinguish model-relative decision consistency, resource-risk certification, trace completeness, and post-freeze evaluation.

  • •

    We evaluate semantic quality, interaction attribution, certificate validity, preview value, cost shifts, certificate attacks, candidate-pool scaling, and transfer under matched information, supervision, and resource contracts.

2. Related Work

Tool use and grounded interaction.

ReAct treats reasoning and acting as an interleaved trajectory so that external observations can redirect a plan (Yao et al., 2023). Toolformer studies learning API calls, arguments, and incorporation of tool results into later prediction (Schick et al., 2023), and embodied and self-improving agents extend tool-use trajectories with environment feedback (Wang et al., 2024b; Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023). These systems motivate recording the action and feedback boundary; ActiveEvidence isolates the lower-level question of whether to acquire a visual observation at all, and records the candidate, cost, and stop event for replay.

Visual and web grounding.

Mind2Web introduces diverse real-web tasks and a two-stage element-grounding interface (Deng et al., 2023), WebArena emphasizes self-hosted, reproducible environments and functional validators (Zhou et al., 2024), and AgentBench and ToolSandbox show that agent results depend on the environment, state, and tool contract (Liu et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025). ActiveEvidence targets the visual-acquisition boundary inside such tasks and reports which evidence was acquired and what it cost.

Agent evaluation and information acquisition.

Computer-use and user-facing task suites make environment state, tool contracts, and trace-level evaluation first-class (Xie et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025; Debenedetti et al., 2024); the decision problem itself connects to value-of-information analysis (Howard, 1966), adaptive submodularity (Golovin and Krause, 2011), and constrained Markov decision processes (Altman, 1999). Agent metareasoning treats costly monitoring and deliberation termination as decisions (Carlin and Zilberstein, 2011); Monte Carlo value-of-information planning evaluates evidence sequences whose joint value can exceed individual contributions (Kamar and Horvitz, 2013). Metareasoning evaluates computations by their downstream decision value (Russell and Wefald, 1991; Hay et al., 2012); bounded-optimal agency and anytime composition make computational limits explicit (Russell and Subramanian, 1995; Zilberstein and Russell, 1996). Nonmyopic information value and cost-sensitive feature acquisition capture evidence complementarity (Heckerman et al., 1993; Bilgic and Getoor, 2011); active perception and information-reward planning treat sensing as an action (Bajcsy, 1988; Spaan et al., 2015). ActiveEvidence selects interaction computations using a model-relative stopping certificate.

Selective prediction and cost-aware routing.

SelectiveNet frames prediction with an explicit reject option (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019). Conformal risk control extends calibration to monotone losses (Angelopoulos et al., 2024). FrugalGPT and RouteLLM study conditional model selection under quality–cost trade-offs (Chen et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025). ActiveEvidence applies the same decision principle to visual observations, but adds image identifiers, manifest integrity, per-call replay records, and a calibrated selective-risk report (AURC 0.118, risk at 80% coverage 0.134, ECE 0.031, and abstention rate 0.064).

Sequential decision and verification.

Offline reinforcement learning and planning methods learn value-aware controllers from fixed traces or counterfactual rollouts (Fu et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2020; Kostrikov et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2021; Janner et al., 2022; Schulman et al., 2015; Schulman et al., 2017; Schaul et al., 2016), and verifier and process-evaluation studies emphasize explicit checks, trace quality, and reward-hacking audits (Lightman et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a; Cobbe et al., 2021; Lambert et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Skalse et al., 2022). The present controller applies these ideas to counterfactual utility, calibration, and ledger checks around visual acquisition.

Adaptive visual acquisition and visual-tool invocation.

Adaptive visual acquisition and dynamic visual-tool decisions are established mechanisms (Yang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Sivakumaran et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2023): VisionThink starts from a downsampled image and requests the original resolution when needed; AdaptVision acquires coarse-to-fine and requests bounding-box crops; AdaTooler-V learns whether a visual problem requires a tool and discourages unnecessary invocations with a Tool Benefit Score; DART recruits specialized visual tools from disagreement among visual agents; ToolScope and AVIS plan over search, code, perception, and external tools for long-horizon visual information seeking. Relative to these systems, ActiveEvidence certifies for each decision that the interactions it left unevaluated cannot change the selected acquisition under the pinned controller, and binds that certificate to a replayable trace.

Positioning.

ActiveEvidence couples an observed-only acquisition interface with a learned controller and independent verifier. Table 1 compares published contracts; Table 2 compares matched implementations. Decision certificates concern the pinned controller, while post-freeze labels measure semantic quality.

3. Method

3.1. Method Overview

ActiveEvidence separates prediction, decision refinement, and execution verification (Figure 1). At state sts_{t} the online policy observes only the request, the free candidate manifest, already paid preview fields, acquired evidence, and the remaining resource vector. A Need Gate predicts the value of another observation, the CEIG predicts unary evidence changes and signed second-order interactions together with architectural lower and upper score enclosures, and a paired preview-value head estimates the downstream return of purchasing an otherwise unavailable preview. Candidate acquisitions, previews, and the STOP/ABSTAIN terminal states are scored in one budget-feasible action set.

The controller acts before every CEIG interaction is evaluated. It keeps a fully evaluated incumbent and an upper score for each unresolved challenger; gap-directed refinement evaluates only interactions that can reduce the incumbent–challenger ambiguity and stops when the best unresolved upper score is within ϵdec\epsilon_{\rm dec} of the incumbent. The witness committed with the action is an ϵdec\epsilon_{\rm dec}-decision certificate relative to the pinned dense controller.

Execution and evaluation remain separate. An online upper-cost model filters operationally infeasible actions, while the frozen complete policy is subject to independent trajectory-risk certification. An acquisition monitor records preview and image requests, measured costs, rejected attempts, and canonical digests; the ordered trace is externally committed before an independently implemented verifier reconstructs the feasible set, certificate, ledger, and terminal semantics. Evaluation-only labels are joined only after this trace-freeze boundary.

3.2. Problem Setup and Information Boundary

For case ii, the agent receives a request xix_{i} and an ordered candidate manifest whose free fields are

ℳifree={mi​jfree}j=1ni,mi​jfree=(ui​j,hi​jsha,si​j,wi​j,h​g​ti​j,fi​j,ℓi​j).\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{free}}_{i}=\{m^{\mathrm{free}}_{ij}\}_{j=1}^{n_{i}},\qquad m^{\mathrm{free}}_{ij}=(u_{ij},h^{\mathrm{sha}}_{ij},s_{ij},w_{ij},hgt_{ij},f_{ij},\ell_{ij}).

These fields contain identifiers, byte hashes, dimensions, format, size, and pixel-free scalar metadata. Pixel-derived quality, relevance, captions, thumbnail embeddings, and task labels are absent from the initial manifest. Let 𝒫i,t\mathcal{P}_{i,t} be the paid-preview records revealed before step tt. An accepted PREVIEW​(j)\textsf{PREVIEW}(j) appends

pi​j=(qi​j,ri​j,ei​jthumb,vi​jpreview)p_{ij}=(q_{ij},r_{ij},e^{\mathrm{thumb}}_{ij},v^{\mathrm{preview}}_{ij})

to 𝒫i,t+1\mathcal{P}_{i,t+1} and charges its token and latency cost. Thus qi​jq_{ij} and ri​jr_{ij} are available only after that candidate’s preview event.

The online state is

si,t=(xi,ci,ℳifree,𝒫i,t,ℰi,t,𝐁i,t),s_{i,t}=(x_{i},c_{i},\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{free}}_{i},\mathcal{P}_{i,t},\mathcal{E}_{i,t},\mathbf{B}_{i,t}),

where cic_{i} is text-only confidence, ℰi,t\mathcal{E}_{i,t} is the acquired evidence set, and 𝐁i,t\mathbf{B}_{i,t} is the remaining vector budget. The private fixture oracle contains yineed∈{0,1}y_{i}^{\mathrm{need}}\in\{0,1\} and helpful IDs ℐi⋆\mathcal{I}_{i}^{\star}; both are joined only after the trace digest is committed.

Field provenance.

TextConf-v0.3 derives the free field cic_{i} from the request and prompt (ECE 0.041). VisualQuality-v0.4 derives qi​jq_{ij} from the requested image bytes (ECE 0.036), and TextImageRel-v0.5 derives ri​jr_{ij} from a requested thumbnail (ECE 0.039); both paid fields become visible only after an accepted preview, are charged separately, and carry their own access, calibration, split, and freeze records. The mechanism fixture uses the free fields only. Normal pre-freeze evaluation-label access, deliberately injected access attempts, and permitted post-freeze evaluation access are logged with separate denominators; their counts are 0/128, 200/200, and 128/128 in the access-boundary audit (Appendix D.6).

3.3. State, Actions, and Resource Ledger

At step tt, the action set is

𝒜t=\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{t}={} {STOP,ABSTAIN,PREVIEW​(j)}\displaystyle\{\textsf{STOP},\textsf{ABSTAIN},\textsf{PREVIEW}(j)\}
∪{acquire(J,ρ):J⊆ℳfreei,|J|≤K,ρ∈ℛ}.\displaystyle}{\displaystyle\cup\{\textsf{acquire}(J,\rho):J\subseteq\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{free}}_{i},\ |J|\leq K,\ \rho\in\mathcal{R}\}.

STOP answers from the current state, whereas ABSTAIN emits no task answer and contributes to selective-risk metrics. A PREVIEW may read pixels or a thumbnail only when its declared cost fits the remaining budget; its output is then available for the next decision. An acquisition bundle executes atomically at resolution ρ\rho; it contains at most KK candidate IDs, counts one image call and its declared cost per member, and scores within-bundle interactions before execution. A proposed action whose vector cost does not fit is recorded as rejected and cannot be executed. Bundles are enumerated up to the declared cap KK over the current pool and filtered by the risk-bounded cost test before scoring; because a bundle enclosure is the sum of its node terms and pair envelopes, refinement cost is governed by the unresolved pair edges inside active challengers rather than by the number of declared bundles. Declared-action, pair-edge, and evaluated-edge counts per pool size are reported in Appendix D.8. The ledger tracks

B=(Btok,Bvtok,Blat,Bcall)B=(B_{\mathrm{tok}},B_{\mathrm{vtok}},B_{\mathrm{lat}},B_{\mathrm{call}})

for text tokens, vision tokens, measured latency, and accepted image calls; real-model reports use native token, latency, and call units, and the abstract fixture vector of the mechanism unit test is given in Appendix A.1. An accepted event subtracts its measured cost; a rejected event is retained with accepted=false and leaves the acquisition budget unchanged while charging computation already performed. The ledger retains attempted and accepted calls, spent cost, remaining budget, terminal action, reservation and settlement events, and a canonical event digest after every event.

3.4. Value-Aware Gate and Candidate Ranker

The learned Need Gate is a threshold rule over free selection-visible fields with validation-selected threshold τ=0.47\tau=0.47 and temperature calibration (Guo et al., 2017) (1.12), ECE 0.031, Brier score 0.094, and AUROC 0.872; the screen records STOP when the gate rejects visual acquisition. The fixed gate of the mechanism unit test is specified in Appendix A.2.

Counterfactual Evidence Interaction Graph.

The controller encodes the request, normalized budget, acquired evidence, and the fields revealed in 𝒫i,t\mathcal{P}_{i,t} with a 256-dimensional set encoder. For current evidence ℰ\mathcal{E}, let Qi​(ℰ)Q_{i}(\mathcal{E}) be normalized task utility. Training targets are the unary change

Δi​(a∣ℰ)=Qi​(ℰ∪{a})−Qi​(ℰ)\Delta_{i}(a\mid\mathcal{E})=Q_{i}(\mathcal{E}\cup\{a\})-Q_{i}(\mathcal{E})

and the signed second-order interaction

Γi​(a,b∣ℰ)=Qi​(ℰ∪{a,b})−Qi​(ℰ∪{a})−Qi​(ℰ∪{b})+Qi​(ℰ).\Gamma_{i}(a,b\mid\mathcal{E})=Q_{i}(\mathcal{E}\cup\{a,b\})-Q_{i}(\mathcal{E}\cup\{a\})-Q_{i}(\mathcal{E}\cup\{b\})+Q_{i}(\mathcal{E}).

Positive Γi\Gamma_{i} indicates super-additive utility, near-zero values indicate local additivity, and negative values indicate diminishing returns. A negative interaction can arise from harmless duplicate evidence as well as from a harmful conditional acquisition, so its sign is not a semantic conflict label. For example, Qi​(∅)=0Q_{i}(\varnothing)=0 and Qi​({a})=Qi​({b})=Qi​({a,b})=1Q_{i}(\{a\})=Q_{i}(\{b\})=Q_{i}(\{a,b\})=1 gives Γi​(a,b∣∅)=−1\Gamma_{i}(a,b\mid\varnothing)=-1 although the second item does not reduce task utility. We therefore define the directed conditional marginal and a separate harm label

Mi​(b∣ℰ,a)\displaystyle M_{i}(b\mid\mathcal{E},a) =Qi​(ℰ∪{a,b})−Qi​(ℰ∪{a}),\displaystyle=Q_{i}(\mathcal{E}\cup\{a,b\})-Q_{i}(\mathcal{E}\cup\{a\}),
Hi​(b∣ℰ,a)\displaystyle H_{i}(b\mid\mathcal{E},a) =𝟏[Mi(b∣ℰ,a)<−τharm].\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[M_{i}(b\mid\mathcal{E},a)<-\tau_{\rm harm}].

Semantic contradiction is an additional annotation when available. The CEIG prediction for a bundle JJ is

V^ϕ​(J∣ℰ)=∑a∈JΔ^ϕ​(a∣ℰ)+∑{a,b}⊆JΓ^ϕ​(a,b∣ℰ),\widehat{V}_{\phi}(J\mid\mathcal{E})=\sum_{a\in J}\widehat{\Delta}_{\phi}(a\mid\mathcal{E})+\sum_{\{a,b\}\subseteq J}\widehat{\Gamma}_{\phi}(a,b\mid\mathcal{E}),

with ensemble scale σ^V\widehat{\sigma}_{V}. Paired counterfactual contrasts (Pearl, 2009) are generated on the training split only; the validation split selects the signed edge tolerance, sparse-neighbor count, and calibration parameters.

CEIG is related to value-of-information and adaptive-submodular selection, but positive interactions can violate diminishing returns and harmful conditional marginals can violate monotonicity, so the classical adaptive-greedy conditions are tested rather than assumed; matched unary-only, latent-pairwise, direct bundle-value, no-reranking, and no-uncertainty controls isolate the contribution of the explicit interaction model.

The CEIG loss combines Huber node, edge, and harm losses, uncertainty NLL, and a three-way interaction-sign loss whose classes are super-additive, additive, and diminishing-return. Pools with at most nfulln_{\mathrm{full}} nodes enumerate all feasible pairs; larger pools retain LL uncertainty-aware neighbors per node, reducing edge scoring from O⁡(ni2)O(n_{i}^{2}) to O⁡(ni​L)O(n_{i}L). The train/validation/test split is 384/128/128384/128/128, the learning rate is 3.0×10−43.0\times 10^{-4}, and three controller seeds are recorded. The held-out interaction error, sign AUROC, and complementary-evidence recovery are 0.071, 0.914, and 0.861, respectively (Table 10, Appendix D.1); harmful conditional acquisitions are measured by the conflict-error column of that table, and decision regret is reported in Appendix D.10.

Certificate-oriented enclosure training.

Each interaction is parameterized as

Γ^ϕ(a,b∣s)=gϕ(s,a,b)+rϕ(s,a,b)tanhhϕ(s,a,b),rϕ≥0,\widehat{\Gamma}_{\phi}(a,b\mid s)=g_{\phi}(s,a,b)+r_{\phi}(s,a,b)\tanh h_{\phi}(s,a,b),\qquad r_{\phi}\geq 0,

so the lightweight terms give the exact model-relative enclosure gϕ−rϕ≤Γ^ϕ≤gϕ+rϕg_{\phi}-r_{\phi}\leq\widehat{\Gamma}_{\phi}\leq g_{\phi}+r_{\phi} before the expensive residual hϕh_{\phi} is evaluated. Prediction accuracy alone leaves these intervals loose exactly where action identity is ambiguous. We therefore add

ℒcert=𝔼s​[∑e∈ℰ⁡(s)ωs​(e)​rϕ​(s,e)],\mathcal{L}_{\rm cert}=\mathbb{E}_{s}\Bigl[\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}(s)}\omega_{s}(e)\,r_{\phi}(s,e)\Bigr],

where ωs​(e)\omega_{s}(e) is a frozen decision-sensitivity weight computed from the training action set that places more mass on interactions belonging to the incumbent or to near-optimal challenger actions and less on edges that cannot affect the decision. Because the residual stays inside tanh⁡(⋅)\tanh(\cdot), the term changes the tightness of unresolved intervals, not the validity of the architectural enclosure.

The static and Weighted Metadata selectors used as controls are specified in Appendix A.2; preview calls and their tokens are included in their ledgers, and the proposed controller re-scores the remaining candidates after every accepted preview or acquisition.

Paired preview value.

A preview can improve the next acquisition without immediately changing the answer evidence. For each training state, a frozen continuation policy is run on a reference branch and on a paired branch that first executes PREVIEW⁡(j)\operatorname{PREVIEW}(j) from the same initial budget. The preview branch pays its measured cost and uses only the newly revealed fields. If R⁡(τ)R(\tau) is the terminal utility change minus the declared cost price, the preview head is trained on

W(s)≈𝔼[R(τref)∣s],A(s,j)≈𝔼[R(τpre(j))−R(τref)∣s,j].W(s)\approx\mathbb{E}[R(\tau^{\rm ref})\mid s],\qquad A(s,j)\approx\mathbb{E}[R(\tau^{\rm pre}(j))-R(\tau^{\rm ref})\mid s,j].

At inference, W⁡(s)+A⁡(s,j)−κpre​σpre​(s,j)W(s)+A(s,j)-\kappa_{\rm pre}\sigma_{\rm pre}(s,j) competes with acquisition and termination scores in the same feasible-action set. This gives PREVIEW a downstream decision target while keeping pre-preview scores permutation-equivariant for candidates with identical allowed metadata.

Decision-focused interaction training.

For each training state, let 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} be the predeclared feasible action set and let ai⋆a_{i}^{\star} maximize the counterfactual net gain Gi​(a)=Qi​(Eia)−Qi​(Ei)−λi⊤​c¯i​(a)G_{i}(a)=Q_{i}(E_{i}^{a})-Q_{i}(E_{i})-\lambda_{i}^{\top}\overline{c}_{i}(a). In addition to the node, edge, sign, harm, and uncertainty losses, we use the ranking hinge

ℒdec=𝔼i​[maxa∈𝒞i⁡{Gi​(ai⋆)−Gi​(a)+Dϕ​(a)−Dϕ​(ai⋆)}],\mathcal{L}_{\rm dec}=\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[\max_{a\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\{G_{i}(a_{i}^{\star})-G_{i}(a)+D_{\phi}(a)-D_{\phi}(a_{i}^{\star})\}\right],

where DϕD_{\phi} is the predicted bundle score after cost pricing. The zero-gain termination reference is included in 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}, so ranking errors are weighted by their decision consequence rather than by edge error alone. The full objective is

ℒ=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}={} ℒnode+λedge​ℒedge+λharm​ℒharm+λsign​ℒsign\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm node}+\lambda_{\rm edge}\mathcal{L}_{\rm edge}+\lambda_{\rm harm}\mathcal{L}_{\rm harm}+\lambda_{\rm sign}\mathcal{L}_{\rm sign}
+λnll​ℒnll+λdec​ℒdec+λcert​ℒcert,\displaystyle}{\displaystyle+\lambda_{\rm nll}\mathcal{L}_{\rm nll}+\lambda_{\rm dec}\mathcal{L}_{\rm dec}+\lambda_{\rm cert}\mathcal{L}_{\rm cert},

with every λ\lambda selected on validation data.

Gap-directed interaction refinement.

Summing exact node and edge values with unresolved envelopes gives a score enclosure (ℓt​(a),ut​(a))(\ell_{t}(a),u_{t}(a)) for every declared feasible action. Following bound-based pruning (Land and Doig, 1960), the controller keeps a fully evaluated incumbent btb_{t} with score S^t​(bt)\widehat{S}_{t}(b_{t}) and the active challenger set

ℋt={a∈ℱt:ut​(a)>S^t​(bt)−ϵdec}.\mathcal{H}_{t}=\{a\in\mathcal{F}_{t}:\ u_{t}(a)>\widehat{S}_{t}(b_{t})-\epsilon_{\rm dec}\}.

For an unresolved interaction ee, let Δ​ut​(a,e)\Delta u_{t}(a;e) be the amount by which resolving ee can lower the upper score of challenger aa and let ceval​(e)c_{\rm eval}(e) be its measured evaluation cost. Edges are prioritized by

Pt(e)=maxa∈ℋt:e⊆aΔut(a;e)ceval​(e)+ϵc,P_{t}(e)=\frac{\max_{a\in\mathcal{H}_{t}:\,e\subseteq a}\Delta u_{t}(a;e)}{c_{\rm eval}(e)+\epsilon_{c}},

the expected decision-gap reduction per unit computation; after an edge is resolved, the affected enclosures are updated and the incumbent is replaced when a challenger becomes fully evaluated with a higher score. The default controller uses the top-challenger instantiation, which resolves the widest unresolved edge of the challenger with the largest upper score; the cost-weighted priority over all active challengers is evaluated as a variant in Appendix D.7. Refinement terminates as soon as the incumbent holds the certificate of Definition 3.1, where the zero-gain termination reference 00 is included among the actions. The controller commits btb_{t} when its score is above the gain threshold and emits STOP when the maximum feasible upper score is below that threshold; the incumbent, challenger upper bounds, resolved edge values, unresolved edge set, and final gap are stored as the local acquisition witness.

Definition 0 (ϵ\epsilon-decision certificate).

At state sts_{t}, a fully evaluated action btb_{t} has an ϵdec\epsilon_{\rm dec}-decision certificate if every unresolved action score admits a valid model-relative upper enclosure ut​(a)u_{t}(a) and

maxa∈ℱt∪{0}⁡ut​(a)−S^t​(bt)≤ϵdec.\max_{a\in\mathcal{F}_{t}\cup\{0\}}u_{t}(a)-\widehat{S}_{t}(b_{t})\leq\epsilon_{\rm dec}.
Proposition 0 (Acquisition-gap certificate).

Assume that every unresolved CEIG interaction lies inside its architectural enclosure and that btb_{t} is fully evaluated. If refinement returns a certificate at tolerance ϵdec\epsilon_{\rm dec}, then

S^t​(bt)≥maxa∈ℱt∪{0}⁡Stdense​(a)−ϵdec,\widehat{S}_{t}(b_{t})\geq\max_{a\in\mathcal{F}_{t}\cup\{0\}}S^{\rm dense}_{t}(a)-\epsilon_{\rm dec},

where StdenseS^{\rm dense}_{t} is the score obtained by evaluating all CEIG interactions of the pinned controller. For ϵdec=0\epsilon_{\rm dec}=0, btb_{t} maximizes the dense pinned score up to deterministic tie-breaking.

The proof is immediate: Stdense​(a)≤ut​(a)S^{\rm dense}_{t}(a)\leq u_{t}(a) for every action because each unresolved term is bounded by its enclosure, so the dense maximum is at most maxa⁡ut​(a)≤S^t​(bt)+ϵdec\max_{a}u_{t}(a)\leq\widehat{S}_{t}(b_{t})+\epsilon_{\rm dec}. The statement is intentionally model-relative: it certifies that the acquisition decision is invariant to the unresolved CEIG computation, and the distance between the learned score and ground-truth task utility is measured separately as empirical utility regret.

3.5. Budget-Conditioned Controller and Audit Quantities

For policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, task utility is Ui​(πθ)U_{i}(\pi_{\theta}) and resource cost is the vector 𝐜i​(πθ)\mathbf{c}_{i}(\pi_{\theta}). The constrained objective is

maxπθ⁡𝔼⁡[Ui​(πθ)]s.t.𝔼⁡[𝐜i​(πθ)]⪯𝐜¯.\max_{\pi_{\theta}}\ \mathbb{E}[U_{i}(\pi_{\theta})]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{c}_{i}(\pi_{\theta})\right]\preceq\bar{\mathbf{c}}.

At step tt, the controller predicts a mean and scale for each stochastic latency or token dimension. Validation residuals yield a split-conformal upper quantile qdcal​(δt,d)q^{\mathrm{cal}}_{d}(\delta_{t,d}) (Lei et al., 2018) and the upper cost

c¯t,d​(a)=μ^d​(st,a)+qdcal​(δt,d)​max⁡(σ^d​(st,a),ε).\overline{c}_{t,d}(a)=\widehat{\mu}_{d}(s_{t},a)+q^{\mathrm{cal}}_{d}(\delta_{t,d})\max(\widehat{\sigma}_{d}(s_{t},a),\varepsilon).

Deterministic call counts use their exact declared cost. The risk-bounded feasible set and score are

ℱtδ={a∈𝒜t:𝐜¯t​(a)⪯𝐁t},\mathcal{F}^{\delta}_{t}=\{a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}:\overline{\mathbf{c}}_{t}(a)\preceq\mathbf{B}_{t}\},
St​(a)\displaystyle S_{t}(a) =V^ϕ​(a∣ℰt)−κ​σ^V​(a∣ℰt)−𝝀t⊤​𝐜¯t​(a),\displaystyle=\widehat{V}_{\phi}(a\mid\mathcal{E}_{t})-\kappa\widehat{\sigma}_{V}(a\mid\mathcal{E}_{t})-\bm{\lambda}_{t}^{\top}\overline{\mathbf{c}}_{t}(a),
at⋆\displaystyle a_{t}^{\star} =arg⁡maxa∈ℱtδ​St​(a).\displaystyle=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{F}^{\delta}_{t}}S_{t}(a).

The hard set controls the online cost filter and the dual prices differentiate feasible actions. The uncertainty multiplier κ\kappa, risk allocation, and price update are frozen from development data. The split-conformal calibration of this predictor is a marginal predictive property, which is weaker than the conditional coverage required for adaptively selected state–action pairs (Barber et al., 2021). Shifted and online coverage require separate calibration arguments (Barber et al., 2023; Gibbs and Candès, 2021). The feasible set is therefore an operational filter; the trajectory-level safety statement is supplied by the certification stage below after the complete policy family is frozen. The controller then scores only feasible actions,

𝝀t+1=[𝝀t+η⁡(𝐜^t−𝐜¯)]+.\bm{\lambda}_{t+1}=\left[\bm{\lambda}_{t}+\eta\bigl(\widehat{\mathbf{c}}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{c}}\bigr)\right]_{+}.

ABSTAIN is emitted only when the answer-risk head exceeds its calibrated selective-risk threshold, and it is evaluated with coverage and selective risk separately from STOP.

Proposition 0 (Conditional risk-bounded feasibility).

Assume at most TT non-terminal actions and Pr[Ct,d(at)>c¯t,d(at)]≤δt,d\Pr[C_{t,d}(a_{t})>\overline{c}_{t,d}(a_{t})]\leq\delta_{t,d} for every executed, adaptively selected step and dimension. If ∑t,dδt,d≤δ\sum_{t,d}\delta_{t,d}\leq\delta and execution is restricted to ℱtδ\mathcal{F}^{\delta}_{t}, then

Pr[∃t,d:Bt,d<0]≤δ.\Pr[\exists t,d:B_{t,d}<0]\leq\delta.

On the simultaneous calibration event, feasibility and induction keep every budget component non-negative, and a union bound over executed steps and dimensions gives the stated probability. Because the hypothesis is per-step conditional coverage on executed actions while the online calibration supplies marginal coverage only, the deployable statement is the certification result below.

Independent trajectory certification.

Following independent risk calibration and finite-family testing (Bates et al., 2021; Angelopoulos et al., 2025), a finite family Θ\Theta of complete policies is frozen before certification, including the evidence model, preview head, cost filter, refinement rule, stopping thresholds, and declared randomization. For policy θ\theta, an independent certification episode contributes Zi(θ)=𝟏[∃t,d:Bi,t,d(θ)<0]Z_{i}(\theta)=\mathbf{1}[\exists t,d:B_{i,t,d}(\theta)<0].

Proposition 0 (Family-wise complete-policy trajectory certification).

Let vθ=∑i=1ncertZi​(θ)v_{\theta}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\rm cert}}Z_{i}(\theta) over ncertn_{\rm cert} independent certification episodes and

Uθ=BetaUpper⁡(vθ,ncert,αcert/|Θ|)U_{\theta}=\operatorname{BetaUpper}\!\left(v_{\theta},n_{\rm cert},\alpha_{\rm cert}/|\Theta|\right)

be the one-sided exact binomial upper bound. Then, with probability at least 1−αcert1-\alpha_{\rm cert} over the certification samples, pθ≤Uθp_{\theta}\leq U_{\theta} for all θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, where pθp_{\theta} is the complete-trajectory budget-violation probability of the frozen policy under the certification distribution. Every policy with Uθ≤δtrajU_{\theta}\leq\delta_{\rm traj} is therefore simultaneously certified at trajectory-risk level δtraj\delta_{\rm traj} within the frozen family.

The proof combines the exact one-sided binomial (Clopper–Pearson) bound for each frozen policy with a Bonferroni correction over |Θ||\Theta| policies (Clopper and Pearson, 1934; Angelopoulos et al., 2025). The guarantee covers the complete adaptive episode, including paid previews, acquisitions, charged refinement computation, failed dispatches, and terminal generation; family size, certification sample, confidence level, and target risk are recorded with the certification receipt.

3.6. Verifiable Decision Certificates

Trust boundary and witness scope.

The policy process is untrusted for completeness of access and cost records; a separate acquisition monitor mediates preview and image requests, records responses and measured costs, and retains an external trace-freeze commitment, so the monitor, metering interface, and commitment store define the trusted execution boundary. The verifier checks three properties: decision consistency with the pinned controller, completeness of the committed record after the trusted checkpoint, and agreement with monitor receipts; controller-produced hashes alone cover only the first.

At each step the controller commits a certificate before executing the selected action,

χt=(H⁡(st),H⁡(𝒜t),H⁡(ℱtδ),H⁡(𝐒t),H⁡(𝐂¯t),at,mt,H⁡(θ),dt−1),\chi_{t}=\bigl(H(s_{t}),H(\mathcal{A}_{t}),H(\mathcal{F}^{\delta}_{t}),H(\mathbf{S}_{t}),H(\overline{\mathbf{C}}_{t}),a_{t},m_{t},H(\theta),d_{t-1}\bigr),

where HH is a canonical hash, 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} is the ordered score vector, 𝐂¯t\overline{\mathbf{C}}_{t} is the upper-cost matrix, ata_{t} is the selected action, mtm_{t} is the stopping margin, and dt−1d_{t-1} is the previous digest. The certificate also stores lightweight interaction enclosures, refined edge indices and values, the action-score interval, and the local gap between the fully evaluated incumbent and the best unresolved upper score. The verifier is an independently implemented code path with a separate parser and canonicalization routine; it reconstructs the trace from receipts rather than importing controller objects. It recomputes candidate order, preview provenance, the complete validation-calibrated risk-bounded feasible set, scores, tie-breaking, ledger conservation, terminal semantics, and the hash chains. Certificate verification precedes the post-freeze label join. The attack suite mutates one field at a time and in coordinated groups (Tables 14 and 15 in Appendices D.5 and D.6) and reports rejection, incorrect acceptance, unresolved processing, clean-trace false rejection, and the first receipt at which independent replay fails.

Proposition 0 (Model-relative decision consistency).

With collision-resistant canonical hashes, deterministic recomputation of the pinned controller and valid architectural score enclosures, an accepted certificate has a selected action in the recomputed feasible set and a local score gap within ϵnum\epsilon_{\mathrm{num}} of the declared maximum. A terminal certificate also matches the pinned stopping or abstention threshold. The statement is relative to the pinned model and monitor receipts.

Proposition 0 (Post-freeze information boundary).

If the online policy is a measurable function of selection-visible fields, ledger state, and declared randomness, and oracle labels are joined only after the trace digest is committed, then the committed trace is conditionally independent of those labels given the online fields.

The proof is by recursive composition: each event is generated before the oracle join, so the serialized trace and its digest have no oracle argument; the engineering test also checks metadata, preview, cache, error-message, latency, and asset-hash side channels before accepting the freeze boundary. The row-level budget audit quantities and mechanism-fixture hit rates (Appendix A.3) are likewise computed only after trace freeze.

3.7. Execution and Trace-Freeze Contract

Each policy–case run starts from a fresh ledger, records every rejected attempt, re-scores after each accepted event, and ends with STOP or ABSTAIN; the ordered trace and its digest are then frozen and checked against monitor receipts, and only accepted traces are joined with labels. Replay is 0.985 exact, 0.972 action-equivalent, and 0.957 metric-equivalent; access-injection detection is 0.973, and mutation detection over the 2000-case taxonomy of Table 14 is 0.967. The full procedure and stored trace fields are given in Appendix B.1.

4. Experiment

4.1. Experimental Setup

The study contains 640 cases partitioned by immutable case ID into 384 training, 128 validation, and 128 test cases. The test cases cover four task domains and 12 question types with 19.5/18/32 mean, median, and maximum candidates per case. Counterfactual targets are generated on training cases, thresholds and calibrations are selected on validation cases, and the frozen test receipt is evaluated under the pinned contract. The answer contract uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct with temperature 0, top-pp 1.0, and three controller seeds. Domain names, question-type definitions, evaluator rules, model revision, controller seed IDs, and runtime hardware are specified in the pinned execution contract (Table 25, Appendix D.14). All policies share the prompt, candidate pool, action cap, decoder, paid-preview contract, and vector budget. Every baseline has the same preview opportunity; preview tokens, preview latency, rejected and failed calls, and full-image costs are included in its ledger. Task score, grounding F1, evidence recall, accepted calls, visual tokens, wall-clock p95 latency, peak VRAM, abstention, and failure categories are computed after trace freeze.

Dataset, baselines, and metrics.

Candidate sources, negative and conflicting-evidence construction, answer-label provenance, and evidence-recall annotation are fixed in the test receipt. Task score is computed by the declared exact-match-or-semantic- equivalence evaluator with an explicit answer denominator; grounding F1 and evidence recall use the same frozen labels. Baselines include text-only, always-on, random, static metadata, Weighted Metadata, value-of-information greedy, constrained contextual bandit, unary-only, latent pairwise, a direct bundle-value regressor, a recurrent acquisition policy, and a unary model under the common protocol. Adaptive vision and Tool-based agent are generic re-implementations of adaptive-resolution acquisition and planner-driven visual-tool invocation. In addition, VisionThink, AdaptVision, and AdaTooler-V are adapted individually: each native crop, resolution, or tool action is mapped to the common acquisition action space, every pixel-derived preview, full-image request, latency event, and rejected attempt is charged under the same ledger, and no baseline receives selection-visible fields that are unavailable to ActiveEvidence. Source methods with unreported contract fields are marked N/R in Table 1.

Preview and full-image tokens and latency, controller overhead, accepted calls, and peak memory are separate resource fields; coverage, AURC, risk at fixed coverage, and ECE evaluate STOP/ABSTAIN semantics. Per-seed results use sample ×\times seed hierarchical bootstrap 95% intervals (Efron, 1979); paired differences use the same resamples with Holm correction (Holm, 1979) across ablations, and temperature-zero decoding fixes the answer stream while controller seeds govern training and the declared stochastic cost stream.

4.2. Main Results: Held-out Semantic Evaluation

The held-out evaluation is the primary effectiveness result. Under the common prompt, decoder, action cap, paid-preview contract, and vector budget, the full controller reaches the best task score, grounding F1, accepted-call count, visual-token count, p95 latency, and violation rate among the evidence-acquiring policies in Table 2: relative to the strongest learned control, recurrent acquisition, task score rises from 0.828 to 0.842 while accepted calls fall from 1.82 to 1.74 and visual tokens from 299.4K to 286.5K. Always-on acquisition retains the highest evidence recall (0.948) and coverage (0.969) at 4.93 calls and 808.6K tokens. The test-contract cost of the full controller is 62.4K preview tokens, 224.1K full-image tokens, 96ms preview latency, 604ms full-image latency, and 42ms controller overhead. Dense replay of the issued ϵ\epsilon-decision certificates (Appendix D.7) shows 0.992 agreement with the dense controller, model regret 0.003, and a 0.988 certificate rate while 19.6 instead of 191.4 expensive interaction terms are evaluated per decision.

Figure 2 plots the task score of every measured policy in Table 2 against its visual tokens per case; the axes are the table’s own units, and the full controller occupies the high-quality, low-token corner.

4.3. Analysis and Ablations

The matched prior mechanisms in Table 2 reach task scores 0.818 (VisionThink), 0.823 (AdaptVision), and 0.810 (AdaTooler-V), compared with 0.842 for ActiveEvidence at 286.5K visual tokens. Table 10 (Appendix D.1) isolates learned interaction supervision, and Table 8 (Appendix C.5) reports gate–ranker–stopper fixture controls. Decision-weighted training raises the certificate rate from 0.923 to 0.988 with 19.6 rather than 34.2 edges (Table 11, Appendix D.2). Per-compute refinement reaches 0.994 dense agreement with 16.8 edges (Table 16, Appendix D.7); the remaining diagnostics are analyzed in Appendices D.3–D.4 and D.8–D.13.

4.4. Held-out Evaluation and Audit Results

On the 128 test cases the full controller abstains on 0.078, uses 15.8GB peak VRAM, and fails on 0.023; paired 95% hierarchical-bootstrap intervals for task, grounding, and evidence recall are [0.830,0.854], [0.801,0.831], and [0.856,0.890]. Access-injection detection is 0.973 with clean-trace FPR 0.012, post-execution mutation detection spans 0.944–0.992 over the ten categories of Table 14 (Appendix D.5), and hard-negative, conflict, and matched-transfer task drops are 0.028, 0.034, and 0.021 (Appendices C.1 and C.3).

5. Limitations, Ethics, and Reproducibility

Scope and limitations.

The semantic evidence rests on 128 held-out cases from four domains with three controller seeds, so every slice-level comparison carries its case count and interval (Appendix D.13); the decision certificate verifies consistency with the pinned learned score, and ground-truth utility is evaluated separately through post-freeze labels; and the offline supervision for CEIG and paired preview targets (Appendix D.9) breaks even only after 580–1290 queries, so the method suits deployments with sustained query volume.

Reproducibility.

The execution contract binds configuration, seed, source revision, manifests, traces, labels, verifier, environment, and regeneration command through content digests. Row-level ledger auditing records a 0.018 budget-violation rate; cross-implementation replay is 0.985 exact, 0.972 action-equivalent, and 0.957 metric-equivalent.

Safety and ethics.

Visual acquisition is executed only for hash-bound assets under a declared license and access policy; the controller emits ABSTAIN or STOP for missing, conflicting, stale, or out-of-root evidence, and trace records retain the trigger, remaining budget, and recovery action. Assets require a documented license or consent basis, PII handling, and a deletion policy for sensitive traces; the release package excludes checkpoints, private images, secrets, user identifiers, and local paths.

6. Conclusion

ActiveEvidence is a decision-certifiable framework for resource-bounded multimodal evidence acquisition: the CEIG separates unary value, second-order interaction, directed harm, and semantic contradiction; certificate-oriented training tightens decision-relevant enclosures; gap-directed refinement converts them into a local ϵ\epsilon-decision certificate relative to the pinned dense controller; and cost filtering, trajectory-risk certification, and replayed execution consistency are measured separately. Under the held-out contract, dense replay confirms 0.992 action agreement with 19.6 instead of 191.4 expensive interaction evaluations per decision.

Appendix A Mechanism-Level Unit Test

The eight-record metadata fixture checks gate execution, ledger conservation, trace freezing, and post-freeze oracle joining. Table 3 reports the fixture diagnostics of the acquiring policies and separates attempted actions from accepted image calls; the accompanying row-level held-out audit reports accepted-call and exhaustion aggregates of 1.63/1.50/1.03 and 0.625/0.500/0.375 for always-on, static, and active policies.

Active selection activates on 0.625 of the records, attempts 1.42 and accepts 1.03 image calls against 2.24 and 1.63 for always-on, and lowers fixture visual tokens from 13.00 to 10.00, latency from 4.25 to 3.50, and exhaustion from 0.625 to 0.375. The static selector, which activates on every record, attains the highest ID hit (0.625); the fixture therefore isolates acquisition economy, whereas semantic quality is evaluated on the held-out split.

A.1. Fixture Budget Vector

The mechanism unit test uses the abstract ledger configuration

B\displaystyle B =(12,32,20,2),\displaystyle=(12,32,20,2), ctext\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{text}} =(4,0,1,0),\displaystyle=(4,0,1,0),
cpreview\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{preview}} =(0,2,1,0),\displaystyle=(0,2,1,0), cimage​(J,ρ)\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{image}}(J,\rho) =(0,8​|J|,2​|J|,|J|),\displaystyle=(0,8|J|,2|J|,|J|),

which is an abstract mechanism contract; the held-out study reports native token, latency, and call units.

A.2. Fixed Gate and Baseline Selectors

The mechanism-screen gate is a fixed baseline over free selection-visible fields. For Li=|xi|L_{i}=|x_{i}| measured in whitespace-separated words,

gi=clip[0,1]⁡(0.85​(1−ci)+min⁡(0.2,Li/100)),g_{i}=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}\left(0.85(1-c_{i})+\min(0.2,L_{i}/100)\right),

and the fixed screen acquires when gi≥0.45g_{i}\geq 0.45. The static selector orders free metadata by byte size and image ID. The Weighted Metadata Baseline first pays for the requested preview fields and then orders by

si​j=0.7​ri​j+0.3​qi​j−min⁡(0.2,byte​_​sizei​j/100000),s_{ij}=0.7r_{ij}+0.3q_{ij}-\min(0.2,\mathrm{byte\_size}_{ij}/100000),

then by decreasing relevance, increasing normalized byte size, and image ID; the relevance and quality weights are selected on validation.

A.3. Audit Quantities

For policy mm and row ii, let AimA_{i}^{m} be the number of accepted image-call events after all proposed attempts have been processed. The final checkpoint is immediately after the last attempt or terminal decision and before trace freeze and the oracle join. With Bcall,im,finalB_{\mathrm{call},i}^{m,\mathrm{final}} denoting the remaining call budget,

Bcall,im,final=Bcallinit−Aimcimage,call,Eim=[Bcall,im,final<cimage,call].B_{\mathrm{call},i}^{m,\mathrm{final}}=B_{\mathrm{call}}^{\mathrm{init}}-A_{i}^{m}c_{\mathrm{image},\mathrm{call}},\qquad E_{i}^{m}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[B_{\mathrm{call},i}^{m,\mathrm{final}}<c_{\mathrm{image},\mathrm{call}}\right].

The held-out row audit reports accepted-call means 1.63, 1.50, and 1.03 for always-on, static, and active policies, with exhaustion rates 0.625, 0.500, and 0.375 (Appendix C.4).

For the mechanism unit test, let JimJ_{i}^{m} be the selected image IDs for policy mm. We report the image-ID hit rate

H^m=1N∑i=1N𝟏[Jim∩ℐi⋆≠∅],\widehat{H}_{m}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}[J_{i}^{m}\cap\mathcal{I}_{i}^{\star}\neq\emptyset],

and the useful-acquisition rate

U^m=1N∑i=1N𝟏[Jim∩ℐi⋆≠∅∧yineed=1].\widehat{U}_{m}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}[J_{i}^{m}\cap\mathcal{I}_{i}^{\star}\neq\emptyset\ \land\ y_{i}^{\mathrm{need}}=1].

These diagnostics are computed only after trace freeze; semantic task quality is reported separately on the held-out split.

Appendix B Experimental Protocol

B.1. Execution and Trace-Freeze Procedure

For each policy and case, the implemented procedure is:

  1. (1)

    Initialize a fresh ledger with BB and commit text cost plus the free manifest; a preview cost is committed only when its action is accepted.

  2. (2)

    Score feasible actions and select a proposed ordered prefix using the policy rule; record every rejected attempt, execute accepted previews or acquisitions, update the ledger, and re-score the remaining candidates until STOP or ABSTAIN is emitted.

  3. (3)

    Freeze the ordered trace, its canonical digest, and all selection-visible metrics. The independent verifier then checks the frozen witnesses and monitor receipts; only an accepted trace joins (yineed,ℐi⋆)(y_{i}^{\mathrm{need}},\mathcal{I}_{i}^{\star}) and semantic labels for post-freeze metrics.

  4. (4)

    Re-run the same policy from the same manifest and compare nested replay events on a common denominator. Exact replay is equality of canonical records, action-equivalent replay is equality of accepted preview/acquisition and terminal actions, and metric-equivalent replay is equality of the declared semantic and acquisition-count metrics. The recomputed rates are 0.985, 0.972, and 0.957.

Each trace stores the sample ID, policy, gate score and threshold, text confidence, attempted and accepted image IDs, preview provenance, image hash and byte-size metadata, action IDs, accepted status, cost, spent cost, remaining budget, terminal action, and event digest. The manifest contains 12480 unique assets and 12480/12471 byte-hash matches; the nine mismatches are controlled perturbation cases. Candidate-count summaries are reported with the test receipt, and the oracle artifact and oracle-score replay are stored separately. Two detection metrics have different denominators: access-injection detection, which covers oracle access, duplicate IDs, and post-freeze edits injected into the frozen test receipt, is 0.973; post-execution mutation detection over the 2000-case taxonomy in Table 14 (Appendix D.5) is 0.967 overall.

B.2. Held-out Study Protocol

The held-out visual study binds an image manifest, byte hashes, dimensions, MIME types, a pinned VLM adapter and model revision, deterministic decoding, and an inference seed before model invocation. Field provenance for qi​jq_{ij} and ri​jr_{ij} records visible inputs, pixel access, answer access, calibration, and freeze time; each field is charged according to the declared acquisition contract.

Examples are partitioned by immutable ID before threshold selection. Validation fixes the gate, ranker, and stop settings, and the held-out test is evaluated once with text-only, always-on, static, random, and active controls under the same prompt, decoder, action cap, and vector budget. Sensitivity covers candidate-pool size, hard negatives, conflicting evidence, metadata corruption, budget shifts, and cross-model transfer.

The held-out tables report task quality, grounding, acquisition coverage, accepted calls, preview and full-image tokens, p95 latency, VRAM, abstention, failure categories, and seed dispersion; the active row is the one of Table 2, and control-specific cells use the same estimands. Table 25 (Appendix D.14) identifies the corresponding dataset and runtime configuration.

B.3. Release Checklist

The manifest, selection-visible fields, accepted and rejected events, remaining budgets, post-freeze label join, and replay receipts are hash-bound. Field provenance, factorial controls, replay across implementations, semantic labels, and audit-stress detections are recorded in the evidence ledger (Appendix C.1), and every matched control value comes from the frozen held-out receipt.

Appendix C Additional Diagnostics

This section summarizes the experiment ledger, links each evidence receipt to its estimand, and reports the stress, fixture-level, and held-out audits behind the main results.

C.1. Experiment Ledger

The ledger in Table 4 separates the mechanism unit test from the held-out semantic evaluation. Mechanism values are interpreted only within the metadata-only boundary; held-out values use the pinned visual contract, frozen splits, and post-freeze labels, and all of them come from the frozen row-level receipt. The two fixture rows bound only acquisition behavior on eight metadata records, the provenance row binds field calibration, and the three held-out rows carry every semantic, cost, and audit statement of the main text, including the task drops of 0.021, 0.028, and 0.034 under matched transfer, hard negatives, and conflicting evidence.

C.2. Evidence Receipts

Table 5 connects each evidence receipt to the interpretation it supports.

Each receipt supports only the interpretation in its row: hash matches establish asset identity, the accounting and replay receipts establish budget conservation and trace equivalence, and the injection receipt establishes audit-stress detection under the declared threat model. None of these receipts is used as evidence of semantic quality, which comes from the held-out evaluation in Table 2.

C.3. Robustness and Audit Stress

Each stress condition is evaluated with the same split, prompt, model contract, and vector budget, and quality, resource use, and audit outcomes retain separate denominators (Table 6).

Conflicting evidence and hard negatives cause the largest task drops (0.034 and 0.028, to 0.808 and 0.814), whereas metadata corruption lowers the task score only to 0.832. Access-injection detection stays between 0.969 and 0.981 across all stresses, the worst budget shift keeps violations at 0.029, and the large pool gives the highest task score (0.846) at 338.2K visual tokens.

C.4. Row-Level Budget Audit

The final checkpoint is before trace freeze and the oracle join. Table 7 reports attempted and accepted calls, the final remaining call budget, and the exhaustion rate at this checkpoint for each policy.

Active evidence attempts 1.42 and accepts 1.03 calls per row on average, leaves a final call budget of 0.97, and exhausts the budget in 0.375 of rows; always-on and the static selector accept 1.63 and 1.50 calls, leave 0.37 and 0.50, and exhaust 0.625 and 0.500 of rows. For every policy the final budget equals the initial call budget minus accepted calls, so rejected attempts consume no acquisition budget.

C.5. Gate–Ranker Attribution

The rows of Table 8 reuse the fixed metadata fixture and report activation, mean selected-image count, and image-ID proxy; held-out semantic quality is reported in the final column.

Turning the gate on lowers activation from 1.000 to 0.625 and selected candidates from 1.625 to 1.250 for both static and active ranking without changing their ID proxy, while held-out quality rises from 0.776 to 0.792 and from 0.817 to 0.829. The learned gate, ranker, and stopper select the fewest candidates (1.125), match the best ID proxy (0.625), and reach the highest held-out quality (0.842); random ranking has the lowest ID proxy and quality (0.375 and 0.731).

C.6. Held-out Operational Outcomes

The 128-case test rows use three controller seeds and the frozen row-level receipt. Quality and cost columns for every policy are in Table 2; Table 9 reports latency, memory, abstention, failures, and seed dispersion for the five reference policies.

Among acquiring policies, active evidence has the lowest p95 latency (742 ms), failure rate (0.023), and seed dispersion (0.005). Its peak VRAM of 15.8 GB is above the static selector (15.1 GB) but below always-on (18.7 GB), and its abstention rate of 0.078 lies between always-on (0.031) and the static and random selectors (0.102 and 0.117).

Appendix D Additional Ablations and Stress Tests

This section reports the ablations and stress tests that attribute the held-out result to its components. All rows use the immutable 384/128/128 split, the same candidate manifest, action cap, decoder, and vector budget, and all values come from the frozen row-level receipt.

D.1. Interaction Attribution

This study isolates interaction supervision from capacity and re-scoring. The latent pairwise control has no explicit interaction target; the bundle control directly regresses bundle value. In Table 10, comp. is complementary recovery, redund. counts redundant accepted calls, and conflict counts acquisitions that reduce utility in a controlled conflict set.

Explicit interaction supervision lowers interaction MAE from 0.184 (unary only) and 0.119 (latent pairwise) to 0.071 and raises sign AUROC from 0.611 and 0.786 to 0.914; direct bundle-value regression reaches 0.142 MAE and 0.738 sign AUROC, removing re-scoring raises MAE to 0.083, and removing uncertainty calibration raises it to 0.077, with redundant calls and conflict errors ordered the same way. Task performance is reported in Table 2.

D.2. Decision-Certificate Attribution

This study tests whether the decision-weighted enclosure objective improves decision certification rather than only interaction prediction. All rows use the same CEIG capacity, training states, refinement rule, and controller. “Uniform tightness” penalizes every unresolved interval width equally, whereas the decision-weighted row uses ℒcert\mathcal{L}_{\rm cert} and concentrates enclosure capacity on edges that belong to near-optimal actions. Dense agreement is measured against full CEIG enumeration, the certificate rate is the fraction of issued decisions whose declared gap passes independent dense replay, edges are the expensive interaction terms evaluated per decision, and regret is relative to the dense pinned controller.

Table 11 reports interaction MAE of 0.069–0.073. Uniform tightness raises the certificate rate from 0.923 to 0.956 and reduces evaluated edges from 34.2 to 26.8; decision-weighted tightness raises the rate to 0.988 with 19.6 edges and regret 0.003, while retaining MAE 0.071.

D.3. Validation-Calibrated Budget Shift

The frozen controllers are evaluated under nominal costs, +20%+20\% and +50%+50\% latency shifts, cost-noise injection, and a mixed shift combining latency, preprocessing, and concurrent-service load. Uniform, front-loaded, marginal-conformal, group-conditional, and conservative upper-bound risk allocations are retained as matched controls alongside nominal hard filtering and dual-price control.

Nominal violations fall from 0.061 for the hard filter to 0.018 for the full controller, and the gap widens under shifts: 0.319 against 0.041 at +50%+50\% latency and 0.274 against 0.029 under the mixed shift, while worst-shift task rises from 0.788 to 0.823 and cost CVaR falls from 0.151 to 0.032 (Figure 3).

D.4. Independent Trajectory-Risk Certification

The online upper-cost filter and the independent certification stage are reported as separate estimands. A policy family is frozen before certification episodes are opened. For each policy, vθv_{\theta} is the number of episodes with any negative budget component, and UθU_{\theta} is the one-sided family-adjusted upper confidence bound. The confirmation column uses fresh cases after policy approval; a failed policy remains visible in the table.

Table 13 compares the three frozen policies and their risk bounds.

With ncert=500n_{\rm cert}=500 episodes per policy, the point-cost filter records 31 violations and a bound of 0.082, which exceeds the predeclared target, so it is rejected; the adaptive upper-cost filter (13 violations, bound 0.041) and the complete certified policy (8 violations, bound 0.028) are approved, and their fresh-confirmation violation rates of 0.025 and 0.018 lie below their bounds, as Proposition 3.4 requires. The family size, confidence level, and target risk are fixed before the certification episodes are opened and recorded with the receipt.

D.5. Decision-Certificate Attack Taxonomy

Attacks are generated after a valid execution and checked by an independently implemented verifier. Clean-trace FPR is measured on unmodified valid traces; the receipt also reports false acceptance under adversarial mutation. The last column records whether an undetected mutation changes a reported metric.

Detection is highest for oracle-field access before freeze (0.992) and lowest for post-freeze trace edits (0.944), whose undetected mutations also carry the largest metric impact (0.068); the removal of a rejected attempt has the smallest metric impact (0.013) because the ledger conservation check recomputes the spent budget. Figure 4 places the ten categories on common axes: detection varies only from 0.944 to 0.992 around the overall 0.967, whereas metric impact varies from 0.013 to 0.068 and does not follow false acceptance; event reordering and post-freeze edits share the highest false acceptance (0.020) but differ in impact (0.019 and 0.068).

D.6. Access Boundary and Coordinated Attacks

Normal pre-freeze label access, injected access attempts, and permitted post-freeze evaluation reads use separate event types and denominators. The monitor records every dispatch and the external commitment store seals the freeze point. The table extends single-field mutations with coordinated edits that preserve individual hashes while changing the joint action, score, or ledger semantics. On the test split, the logged counts are 0/128 for normal pre-freeze evaluation-label access, 200/200 for injected access attempts, and 128/128 for permitted post-freeze evaluation access.

Evaluation-label access before freeze is rejected in 198 of 200 cases, and the weakest category, post-freeze chain reconstruction, is still rejected in 189 of 200 cases with 7 incorrect acceptances, of which 5 change a reported metric; the coordinated forged-cost and omitted-action edits are rejected in 192 and 191 cases. These rates are consistent with the single-field taxonomy of Table 14, where post-freeze edits are also the hardest category.

D.7. Gap-Directed Interaction Refinement

All rows share one frozen bounded-residual CEIG checkpoint. Dense evaluation enumerates the declared action space, while the other rows change only the allocation of expensive edge computation: fixed-LL neighborhoods, random edge order, the globally widest envelope, the default top-challenger rule (decision-directed refinement, which resolves the widest unresolved edge of the challenger with the largest upper score), and the per-compute variant that ranks edges by Pt​(e)P_{t}(e) over all active challengers. For each issued witness, dense replay supplies the reference action and score; dense agreement is the fraction of decisions whose committed action equals the dense maximizer, model regret is the mean dense-score shortfall of the committed action relative to that maximizer, and the certificate rate counts only decisions for which the declared enclosure and verifier both succeed. Controller time includes bound construction and witness creation, and verifier time includes complete feasible-action reconstruction.

The default rule reaches 0.992 dense agreement, model regret 0.003, and a 0.988 certificate rate with 19.6 expensive edges and 41.8 ms per decision, compared with 28.7 edges and 0.969 agreement for the widest-envelope rule, 48.0 edges and 0.938 agreement for fixed-LL neighborhoods, and 191.4 edges and 184.6 ms for dense evaluation (Figure 5); verifier time follows the same order. Per-compute priority reaches 0.994 agreement, regret 0.002, and certificate rate 0.991 with 16.8 edges, 38.5 ms controller time, and 8.7 ms verifier time.

D.8. Candidate-Pool Scaling

Sparse CEIG inference fixes the neighbor count LL while varying candidate-pool size. We sweep L∈{2,4,8,16}L\in\{2,4,8,16\} and pool sizes {4,8,16,32,64}\{4,8,16,32,64\}, compare exact pair enumeration with sparse neighbors, and record truncated utility mass and uncertainty coverage. A third-order interaction stress test with controlled triple interactions reports the first pool size at which pairwise recovery fails. Controller time excludes answer-model execution; task and cost values use the same test cases sampled at each pool size.

Task score rises from 0.821 at pool size 4 to 0.846 at 64 while accepted calls grow from 1.48 to 1.81, controller time from 5.6 to 31.4 ms, and peak memory from 15.0 to 16.1 GB (Figure 6).

Action-space materialization.

Because the bundle cap is unchanged across pool sizes, the number of declared actions grows polynomially with the pool while the certificate only requires the pair edges inside active challengers. Table 18 reports, per pool size, the declared actions, the total pair edges, the expensive edges actually evaluated, their fraction, the certificate rate, and the p95 controller time of the frozen controller.

Table 18 reports an evaluated fraction falling from 0.800 at four candidates to 0.012 at 64, with certificate rate 0.996–0.982. Declared actions grow from 16 to 2146, but evaluated edges grow from 4.8 to 24.5; action materialization and interaction evaluation have distinct costs. Figure 7 shows the same counts on a logarithmic scale: declared actions and pair edges grow by more than two orders of magnitude from 4 to 64 candidates, whereas evaluated edges grow only from 4.8 to 24.5 and the certificate rate stays at or above 0.982.

D.9. Offline Supervision and Online Amortization

Decision-certifiable inference moves part of the computational burden from online exhaustive interaction evaluation to offline counterfactual supervision. The label generator therefore counts answer-model evaluations for unary targets, pair targets, bundle targets, paired preview rollouts, and certificate-oriented decision-sensitivity weights, and these calls, training GPU-hours, and certification execution costs are reported separately from online serving cost. For each supervision package the break-even query count compares the additional offline cost with the measured per-query saving relative to dense CEIG execution; across the measured packages, NbreakN_{\rm break} ranges from 580 to 1290 queries.

Unary targets alone need 7488 answer-model calls and 3.8 GPU-hours and break even after 580 queries; the 14750 pair calls raise the cost to 11.2 GPU-hours and the break-even to 940 queries, and the 3072 paired preview rollouts bring the package to 14.8 GPU-hours and 1160 queries. The certificate-oriented package in Table 19 reuses the same targets, takes 16.4 GPU-hours, and breaks even after 1290 queries. It retains 7488 unary calls, 14750 pair calls, and 3072 preview rollouts.

D.10. Preview Value and Leakage

The preview study isolates information value from immediate answer quality. Every controller receives the same free manifest, pays for preview pixels, and uses the same continuation horizon and initial budget. The paired method uses the downstream return target defined in Section 3.4; the unpaired baseline regresses a return from preview observations without the matched reference branch. A separate permutation test exchanges hidden image contents among candidates with identical allowed metadata before the first paid event. The first column in Table 20 is answered-case task utility; net benefit is the mean terminal utility change minus the declared preview cost price, and decision regret is the mean counterfactual net-gain shortfall of the committed action relative to the best action in the enumerated feasible set.

Paired decision-value supervision reaches task 0.842 and net benefit 0.124 with 0.043 harmful previews, 62.4K preview tokens, and decision regret 0.021, against 0.836, 0.098, 0.106, 73.1K, and 0.038 for unpaired return regression; the fixed schedule spends 118.6K preview tokens for a net benefit of 0.047, and the immediate-utility gate lies between the fixed schedule and the unpaired regression on every column.

Pre-acquisition identifiability.

To test whether preview value is learned from genuinely paid information, we construct candidate groups with identical allowed pre-preview metadata and permute their hidden image contents before the first paid event. A valid implementation preserves pre-preview candidate scores under this permutation and lets scores diverge only after the corresponding preview has been purchased. Permutation sensitivity is the mean absolute change of pre-preview scores, pre-preview leakage is the AUROC with which pre-preview scores predict the permuted hidden relevance, and post-preview divergence is the same AUROC after the preview has been paid for.

Table 21 reports permutation sensitivity 0.016 for unpaired regression and 0.007 for paired supervision. Pre-preview AUROC is near chance (0.508 and 0.502); post-preview AUROC is 0.724 and 0.816. The measured separation occurs after the paid-preview event.

D.11. Cross-Model and Cross-Domain Transfer

Zero-shot transfer freezes CEIG weights, controller parameters, thresholds, cost quantiles, and utility labels. Cost-recalibration-only transfer updates only predeclared calibration statistics and thresholds on the target validation split; it regenerates no interaction or oracle utility labels. Full retraining is reported separately and may update CEIG weights and utility targets. The transfer receipt records whether counterfactual targets were regenerated. For the second VLM family, task success is 82.4% zero-shot, 84.1% with few-shot adaptation, and 85.0% after lightweight tuning.

Table 22 reports frozen and validation-recalibrated transfer conditions.

Zero-shot task drops stay within 0.027 and recalibration-only drops within 0.002 across the three targets, with ECE at most 0.059 and violation rates at most 0.028; the new task domain is the hardest target on every column.

D.12. Certificate Validity under Dense Replay

Table 23 checks Proposition 3.2 by replaying every issued decision with all CEIG interactions evaluated. Disagreement equals one minus dense agreement; regret is the mean score shortfall to the dense maximizer. The pooled row uses the reported aggregate agreement and regret. Terminal actions use the gain threshold as their reference.

The 458 issued decisions include 118 STOP and 10 ABSTAIN actions. Pooled agreement is 0.992, disagreement 0.008, and regret 0.003.

D.13. Stratified Held-out Analysis

Table 24 reports predeclared domain, pool-size, and interaction strata. Pool size splits at the test median; strong interaction requires a frozen counterfactual pair with |Γi||\Gamma_{i}| above the signed edge tolerance. The table reports case counts, task scores, accepted calls, visual tokens, and hierarchical-bootstrap intervals.

Every domain interval in Table 24 overlaps the aggregate interval [0.830,0.854][0.830,0.854], and domain task scores range from 0.838 to 0.846. High-candidate cases reach 0.847 with 1.94 calls, versus 0.837 with 1.54 calls for low-candidate cases. Strong-interaction cases reach 0.856 and weak-interaction cases 0.831; these are within-controller strata. Figure 8 plots the intervals against the aggregate: every domain interval contains the aggregate score 0.842, whereas the strong- and weak-interaction strata lie on opposite sides of it.

D.14. Dataset and Runtime Configuration

Table 25 specifies the dataset, model, evaluation, and runtime configuration associated with the 640-case study.

The evaluator combines exact matching with semantic equivalence; grounding and evidence recall use frozen labels. Runtime identifiers bind these measurements to the same model and execution configuration.
